..
Issued at 145 PM CDT Mon Sep 28 2026

LATE THIS AFTERNOON: Stratus is showing some breaks and lifting
in the clouds through early this evening, more than previously 
anticipated. More sunshine filtering through may allow temperatures
to rise into the low to mid 70s.

TONIGHT AND TUESDAY: Cloudy, mild, rainy weather takes hold tonight 
through at least early Wednesday across the region. Redeveloping and 
thickening evening cloud cover will keep temperatures mild 
overnight, only dropping to around 60 degrees. Broad warm air 
advection ahead of a northern stream shortwave will prompt scattered 
showers and isolated storms to slowly spread east from central SD 
toward the I-29 corridor overnight. A low level pool of moisture up 
to about 3000ft may bring drizzle ahead of the main area of rain, 
but it'll take the sfc low and associated low level jet tracking 
east overnight to saturate dry mid levels. Showers should hold off 
near and east of the I-29 corridor until Tuesday morning, spreading 
east through the day. Despite marginally supportive deep layer shear 
(25-40 kts), weak instability (<500 J/kg) should inhibit severe 
weather threat. Locally heavy rainfall is the main concern thanks to 
our prolonged wet pattern. High confidence (>80%) of most sites 
northwest of a Sioux City to Spencer line will see at least a 
quarter inch of rain Tuesday. Most higher resolution model guidance, 
including the HREF LPMM, suggests a few sites will see a 1+ inches 
of rain by Tuesday evening.

TUESDAY NIGHT THROUGH WEDNESDAY NIGHT: Mid week brings increased 
threat for heavy rain, localized ponding of water on roads and other 
surfaces, and rises on local rivers as an additional few rounds of 
rain progress through the region. Early Tuesday evening, rain should 
sag southeast further into IA, providing some breaks in the rain. 
Overnight through early Thursday, a broad region of widespread, 
persistent showers and isolated thunderstorms is expected to 
overspread much of NE, IA, and portions of far southeast SD and 
southern MN. During this period, stationary front stalls amidst 
broad ascent from the right entrance region of the upper jet and the 
remnants of Hurricane Polo track into the Central U.S. Of particular 
note is the low level jet feeding in moisture-rich, monsoonal air 
with precipitable water values of 1.75-2.00, near the max of 
climatology for this time of year. 

From Tuesday through Thursday morning, an area near and south of a 
Norfolk to Sioux City to Spencer line has a high (>70%+) chance of 
receiving at least 2 inches of rain with potential for a few 
locations to see 4 to 5 inches. Recent model runs continue to wobble 
the heaviest axis of rain anywhere from the Hwy 20 to the I-80 
corridor. This area with the heaviest, most persistent rains 
near/south of a Sioux City to Spencer line has the greater potential 
for any flooding impacts. There is definitely uncertainty in the 
northern extent of the rain as well. While areas near and south of 
Lake Andes to Madison and Pipestone line (including Yankton, Sioux 
Falls, and Worthington) have a high (>60%) chance of receiving over 
an inch of rain from tonight through Thursday morning, locations 
further northwest will be mostly done with rain by Tuesday night, 
missing the later rounds.

THURSDAY THROUGH THE WEEKEND: A strong northern stream cold front 
tracking through late Wednesday night kicks the Desert Southwest 
trough and associated stationary front eastward heading into 
Thursday. Dry air filtering in and surface high pressure passing to 
our north behind the departing system should bring a mostly dry 
Thursday and Friday with increasing sunshine. Thursday brings a 
breezy north wind with cooler air, but we'll see highs hovering 
around 60 degrees both days.

An early look at next weekend shows little to no notable weather 
impacts. Expect mostly dry conditions and a slight warm up for 
Saturday. A passing northern stream front on Saturday night brings a 
very low chance of rain north of I-90, but the main impact looks to 
be a cool down for Sunday.
